content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The contribution of the paper is a method of filtering and planning as joint probabilistic inference. For that, the duality of inference and control is used, such that an adversarial particle filtering approch can be employed. Several experiments that support the claim are presented.

I recommend to reject the paper from publication. Main reasons are the sub-standard presentation of the idea as well as not justifying design decisions.

I find the paper confusing. While the high-level idea is simple, the authors chose not to start the presentations from a reasonable point (i.e., the graphical model) and subsequently introduce the necessary approximations to make the problem tractable, several things are introduced ad hoc. 

E.g. what is the motivation to chose the mean state and the top-M particles? Why was that representation chosen? Were other representations tried? Under what conditions is this representation reasonable, when might it fail? The answers given are not sufficient. 
The text and the algorithm boxes do not serve complementary purposes. Instead, the text merely reiterates what is in the algorithm box. 

Further points for improvement.
- Language. There are grammatical mistakes in the paper, e.g. missing pronouns, some sentences "do not compile", the language is sloppy ("[...] had better be really sampling efficient [...]")
- Eq 1 has two expectations over s. Where does the first s come from? 
- "Only requires a learned Q function" does not seem very "only" to me. These are typically hard to obtain! Also, why is this better than using the true model (which can equally be required to be available) for Monte Carlo approximations?
- When I started reading the paper, I was under the impression that it is about continous time POMDPs. Could be clearer.
- For p(O_t = 1) \propto exp(R) the assumption that R <= 0 is required.
- page 2, paragraph 1: it reads as if the history grew exponentially. I assume the authors were referring to the policy, but that is an unnatural assessment, as policies in continuous spaces are typically continuous as well, making a cardinality argument cumbersome.
- The literature on varitional particle filtering is not respected. Starting points are [1, 2, 3]
- Regression does not imply root mean squared error. Counter example: logistic regression.


References
[1] Gu, Shixiang Shane, Zoubin Ghahramani, and Richard E. Turner. "Neural adaptive sequential monte carlo." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2015.
[2] Naesseth, Christian A., et al. "Variational sequential monte carlo." arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.11140 (2017).
[3] Maddison, Chris J., et al. "Filtering variational objectives." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. 2017.

content.title: Responses to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Many thanks for the review and suggestions.
1. Motivation to choose the mean state and top-M particles.

Since the planning is done in belief space and the belief in our method is represented as a set of particles in the true state space, it is natural to use the top-M particles as an approximated belief representation. During practice, when M is small, this representation itself has a high variance. To mitigate this, we add the mean particle state (the first-order moment). 

For example, imagine our particles concentrate on 2 clusters, if we only sample a few top candidates, it is likely that all sampled particles fall in one cluster. However, by adding the mean, the model has a sense of an overall estimation of the belief. These are the main reasons behind our choice. 

Again, because our state representation is explicit (unlike the latent state in an RNN), we find it natural to use those particles directly. In the experiment we found normally top-3 particles + mean belief is sufficient for planning.

2. Equation 1 has two expectations over $s$.

As mentioned, there are 2 $s$ here. The first $s$ in the outer expectation is the true states sampled from data. The second $s$ denote the particles we have at the current moment. Equation 1 consists of two parts. The first part can roughly be represented as $\log(Z(o | s_\text{real})) + \log(1 - Z(o | \text{particles}))$ and the intuition is to train the observation model to distinguish the real state from the particles. The second part is roughly $\log(1 - Z(o | P(o)))$ and here the intuition is we want the proposer to propose particles similar to the real state.

3. Why using a learned Q function is better than using the true model?

We would like to point out that in the original SMCP paper, equation 3.3 requires estimating the $\log(E_{s_t \sim s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}} [\text{exp}(V(s_t))])$, where the expectation is taking over the possible current state sampled based on the previous state and action. This is harder to approximate. In our equation 2, we do not require such estimation. Since we use soft actor-critic, the Q value is already learned in the policy. Therefore, we just reuse them here. The maximum entropy advantage function is therefore easier to obtain. 
Although we require true states for training the filter, our method doesn’t require a true model of the environment, which we believe is common for most real-world applications. We agree that if we have a true model, planning can become much easier and many conventional Monte Carlo planning methods can apply. However, one of our key novelties is that our method can filter and plan without the true model, by sharing the learned model between the filter and planner and training the two parts jointly. 

4. On page 2, paragraph 1, it reads as if the history grew exponentially.

We did not understand the question very well. The possible history indeed grew exponentially and our method is designed for continuous state and action spaces.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper generalizes the differentiable particle filtering (DPF) to POMDP setting. Moreover, it introduces an extra differentiable SMC component as planner into the model, which together with the DPF will be learned together. The authors demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm on 2D floor positioning, 3D navigation with image input, and Reacher in MuJoCo.

Although the learning through the planner in an end-to-end fashion has been investigated in RL community extensively, e.g., [1, 2], extending it to POMDP is relative novel. However, there are several issues need to be addressed:


1, The optimization objective (1) seems come from nowhere. The motivation of such objective is very unclear. Why this objective is selected? Why not to adapt other alternative objectives, e.g., maximum log-likelihood? Without such justification, the learning target is not convincing. Meanwhile, whether $\psi$ is learned or not. If it is learned, what is the learning objective. 

2, The authors claim that by twisting two SMCs, for planning and state prediction, respectively, the algorithm will lead to better performance. However, after twisting the planner into the learning, the proposed method is only applicable for on-policy setting, while the major advantage of model-based RL is for off-policy. This effect has not been discussed explicitly. I am not sure whether the benefit of the proposed algorithm comes from the coupling of two SMCs or on-policy learning.  

3, The empirical experiments should be improved to be more convincing. One of the major contribution of this paper is using POMDP, rather than traditional MDP. To justify the benefits of the complicated model, a direct comparison between model-free (DQN) model-based (DeepMDP [4] and PlaNet [3]) algorithm upon MDP with same inputs as the inputs of the proposed model is necessary. Moreover, just one MuJoCo is not sufficient to demonstrate the advantages. Please evaluate the proposed algorithm on more environments in standard benchmarks, e.g., MuJoCo and Atari.

Minor:
The terminology "dual" has rigorous definition in math. Please use the terminology following the common knowledge.


1, Okada, Masashi, Luca Rigazio, and Takenobu Aoshima. "Path integral networks: End-to-end differentiable optimal control." arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.09597 (2017).

2, Pereira, Marcus, et al. "Mpc-inspired neural network policies for sequential decision making." arXiv preprint arXiv:1802.05803 (2018).

3, Hafner, D., Lillicrap, T., Fischer, I., Villegas, R., Ha, D., Lee, H., & Davidson, J. (2018). Learning latent dynamics for planning from pixels. arXiv preprint arXiv:1811.04551.

4, Gelada, C., Kumar, S., Buckman, J., Nachum, O., & Bellemare, M. G. (2019). DeepMDP: Learning Continuous Latent Space Models for Representation Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1906.02736.

content.title: Responses to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments.

1. Optimization objective (1)

First, the $\psi$ here is indeed learned; its objective is the conventional mean square regression objective $\text{min} ||s_{t+1} - T_\psi(s_t, a_t)||^2$. As for the objective of the adversarial training, its motivation is explained in the 4th point of our responses to the AnonReviewer1. The main intuition is we would like the proposer to propose reasonable particle states that are like the true state while the observation model (the discriminator) to differentiate true state from proposed particles. As a result, the first part of the objective $(\log Z + \log(1 - Z)) $is for training the observation model while the second part $\log(1 - Z(o, P(o))$ is for training the proposer.

2. On-policy learning

We agree that our method is on-policy. However, every baseline method we propose is also on-policy. Therefore, coupling two SMCs does give us a performance boost. It will be an interesting direction to further extend our method to off-policy learning.

3. Empirical experiments

Thanks for your advice. We would like to mention that the point of using particle filter as the first SMC is due to the partial observability. If the problem reduces to an MDP problem, then our method naturally reduces to SMCP, which in its original paper has already outperformed other baselines in the MDP setting. In addition, the reason why we have not applied our algorithm to benchmarks like Atari is that we focus on explicit state representation. Our particle state lies in the true state space and therefore the model is interpretable and visualizable.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
Summary:
The authors propose Dual Sequential Monte Carlo, a method to jointly perform filtering and planning on continuous POMDPs by nesting two smc filters.

The authors use a variety of pieces in their model. 
First, filtering is used to represent the posterior over current state states (or: belief state).
Second, the authors use the control-as-inference formalism in order to perform planning using SMC by sampling from the posterior of optimal trajectories where optimality is defined via auxiliary binary latent variables proportional to the reward state action pairs yield (and as such trajectories).
Third, the authors propose to use "Adversarial Particle Filtering" as a method to train their observation models.
Fourth, the crucial difference to the main baseline is the inclusion of the mean belief state into the planner by using it both as an auxiliary input for the policy network (as a conditional action prior) and for state propagation during planning. The rationale for this is the hope that this will represent uncertainty in the filter better during planning.

In the experiments, the Dual SMC method tends to outperform the baseline, though at times it is unclear if this is owed to the adversarial model or the actual planner.

Comments:
My main issue with the paper is the role of the mean belief state used for dual smc. This has two major appearances:
1.  I understand the idea that including moments of the state distribution particles together with each individual particle could inform a learned policy network better as to whether states are uncertain or not. However, it is unclear if the first moment is sufficient to do this or if another method would have been more advisable? In the end, little proof is given that this actually achieves the stated goal.
2. The second use of the mean belief state, however, is hard to justify in my opinion. In algorithm 2 line 6, the mean belief state is used to propagate the planner forward given the current action. While I understand that this may save computation compared to using sampled state particles to propagate the posterior forward, this choice ultimately is not principled and causes the planner to be planning for a different model than the one one may want it to plan from, as the state is systematically reset to the mean. This seems to be a particularly optimistic planner and it is unclear how it would respond to multi-modal or long tailed state-spaces during planning. Mainly, it simply is not guaranteed to be planning according to the Bellman equations anymore but generates "some plan" which is close to the model but also departs in a way that is hard to quantify or to have guarantees on. Why change the model during planning?
Why is this choice necessary and what would have been the alternative? What does it buy us?

3. The authors are not doing a good job explaining model training rigorously. A nice way to explain how to train parameters in a state space model while performing SMC on it is via variational inference with adaptive SMC proposal distributions. But even if that were not the chosen way here, the paper is not doing a good job clarifying the objective function for model training.

4. Adversarial Particle Filters are presented as a contribution by the authors. However, these objects have been proposed before and explained, for instance in "Adversarial Sequential Monte Carlo" by Kempinska and Shawe-Taylor. This reference is clearly missing here. In addition, the presentation of the section on adversarial particle filters is confusing. The adversarial training in this case has one role only as far as I can tell: building an implicit observation model in order to achieve more accurate representation of observations through latent states. It would be easy to consider this a particular modeling choice (as opposed to a Gaussian or a Bernoulli observation model), as implicit observation models are quite common in the current probabilistic literature. Presenting it as an adversarial filter is not conveying that accurately.

5. Neural Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo by Shane Gu et al is also a missing reference here.

6. In experiment 2, the model with a density-based observation model (presumably Normal) and Dual SMC wins. Why is the adversarial aspect so important to this paper if it is not even consistently the winning model?

7. I am quite uncomfortable with the missing comparison to a planner that would keep the mean belief state for the policy network but actually plan from the model during the transition T_psi. I would have found that to be the most natural baseline here to also address my comment #2. As it stands, the two main contributions of the paper (adding mean belief state to policy network and planning with mean belief state transitions) are not individually well explained and individually evaluated.

Decision:
The paper proposes an interesting and technically challenging attempt to jointly perform filtering and planning. However, some of the choices in the paper are not well motivated or technically corroborated, as outlined in my comments. I hope the authors can clarify these weaknesses of their paper, as particle-based methods are promising avenues to rigorous model-based planning in POMDPs and the authors are tackling an interesting problem. As the paper stands, I lean towards rejection due to the technical questions about the method.

content.title: Responses to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
Many thanks for the thoughtful review. If you feel we’ve dealt with them well, please consider increasing your score.

1. About the use of the first-order moment.

We agree that including higher-order moments will certainly better capture the belief distribution. In our experiments, we evaluated empirically that the first-order moment (mean) plus a few top-weight particles are sufficient. Unlike previous methods like DVRL, where the particles are latent and the training objective is only the RL objective, our particles are in the real state space and the filter trains them to be close to the true state. As a result, when doing the planning, these particles are supposed to better capture the belief distribution. 
In fact, it is also doable if we remove the first-order moment. The main reason we include the first-order moment is that when we only use a few top-weight particles, there is a larger variance in the resulting belief representation and we would like to add the mean state as compensate.

2. Our method is indeed optimistic. Just like QMDP, our method assumes the uncertainty disappears and plan based on the current belief representation. As a result, we propagate the mean belief state and particles forward for planning. The reason why we assume the uncertainty disappears is that otherwise planning as inference requires modeling the generation of observations, which can be really hard as well as introducing high variance.

3. About the objective functions for modeling training.

There are 5 trainable modules (see Fig. 1). 
1) For the state estimation part, the observation module $Z$ and the particle proposer $P$ follow the minimax training procedure in Eq. (1). 
2) The transition module $T$ is trained to regress the next ground truth state given the current state and action. 
3) For the planning part, the policy module and the critic module are trained in the same way as the original SAC method. 
Due to space constraints, we choose to leave out some objectives in the paper and only keep our own contributions. We will clarify these objective functions rigorously in a future version of this paper. 

4. About the adversarial particle filter.

The technical difference to the existing work “Adversarial SMC” includes:
1) This existing work aims to parameterize a family of generative distributions over observations, thus making them unsuitable for large, complex observation spaces, such as the space of camera images in our experiments. By contrast, what we care more about is the more accurate likelihood values produced by the observation module, which will be used to form the belief representation for the subsequent planning process.
2) Our proposed adversarial particle filter is built upon the recent advances in differentiable particle filters (Karkus et al., 2018b; Jonschkowski et al., 2018). This makes our model be easily combined with other deep networks and adapted to tasks with rich visual inputs. 

3) Our method has a different mathematical form of the training objective function, the proposer and the observation module are jointly learned with the transition module.
Among the recent advances in deep learning, many great models appear to be similar to prior work. Our adversarial filter is driven by a clear motivation, innovative thinking, and strong experimental validation. 

5. Reference “Neural Adaptive...”

Same as the above “Adversarial SMC”, this work also focuses on learning a distribution over observations, which does not fit our cases with rich visual inputs. Unlike these work, our model aims to learn more accurate likelihood to form better belief representations that can lead to more reasonable planning trajectories under observation uncertainty.

6. Whether the adversarial filter is the winning model.

We present the adversarial particle filter for an alternative of multi-modal state estimation, and we believe this method has its value because:
1) It wins in 2 of 3 experiments. 
2) Even for the worst case, it only slightly underperforms its counterpart with density loss in the success rate (95% vs. 97%). In the meanwhile, it achieves a better performance in the step number, indicating that the adversarial filter leads to shorter planning trajectories to solve the POMDPs.
3) We have made it clear that the adversarial particle filter is potential: it can be easily improved by the new advances of the adversarial learning techniques, to avoid mode collapse, or to stabilize training.
We hope this can resolve the concern on the effectiveness of the adversarial particle filter.

7. Comparison with a planner.

We are not sure if we have understood your idea clearly. Do you mean during planning over horizon T, we concatenate the unchanged mean state with the forward propagated particles and then feed them as input to our policy network? If this is the case, we think it is indeed a reasonable baseline of our algorithm, but it also means the policy is dependent on time and thus more difficult to train.

display_title: clarifying my problem with the paper which was unfortunately not addressed with the response

content.title: clarifying my problem with the paper which was unfortunately not addressed with the response
content.comment:
Thank you for your responses.

I  want to point out that my main problem with the paper remains:
during planning, you do not use the model to sample the future.

Let  me quote your response:
"The reason why we assume the uncertainty disappears is that otherwise planning as inference requires modeling the generation of observations, which can be really hard as well as introducing high variance."
That would have been exactly the right thing to compare to, as I was saying earlier.

You replace the transition model with mean-state, effectively treating the model as a deterministic model and crippling the planner to not be able to ever simulate a large space of potential trajectories.
Also: If we had fully deterministic systems, could we not plan more effectively than using dual smc?

The cleanest and most basic form of a planner would use the stochastic model to simulate trajectories. I do not understand why this was not used as a baseline to compare the 'optimistic' planner. It is also not clear to me that you are still performing planning in the 'correct' model given your approach, as you cannot simulate trajectories that lie within the model space. More crucially: your p(s_t+1 | s_t, a_t) will differ between the planner and the model due to the replacement of s_t with mean_bel(s_t) in the former when running forward, which is a real problem that requires careful attention.

I understand this is not a particularly easy experiment to run, but it is nevertheless much more important for the scientific understanding of the core proposed joint filtering-planning process than, for instance, the experiments illustrating the benefits of the implicit likelihood.

Unfortunately for my assessment this means that the most important experiment for the entire paper is missing, which would have been the one comparing to simulating from the actual model given the belief state. I cannot understand if this method actually makes sense or not without at least that comparison, as the technical content is problematic to my eyes for the reasons explained and I would need strong empirical evidence and careful examination on that aspect to overcome that.
